title: Antidotes for toxicological emergencies: A practical review
source: Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2012; 69:199-212 (Primer; Jeanna M. Marraffa, Victor Cohen, and Mary Ann Howland; DOI 10.2146/ajhp110014)
about: A primer in which appropriate therapies for commonly encountered poisonings, medication overdoses, and other toxicological emergencies are reviewed, with discussion of pharmacists' role in ensuring their ready availability and proper use. It states that poisoning is the second leading cause of injury-related morbidity and mortality in the United States, with more than 2.4 million toxic exposures reported each year, and that recently published national consensus guidelines recommend that hospitals providing emergency care routinely stock 24 antidotes. The antidotes discussed, in alphabetical order, are those whose use likely entails the greatest involvement of ED pharmacists: ethanol and fomepizole for toxic-alcohol poisoning; calcium, glucagon and hyperinsulinemia-euglycemia therapy for calcium-channel-blocker and β-blocker toxicities; amyl nitrite, sodium nitrite, sodium thiosulfate and hydroxocobalamin for cyanide; digoxin-specific antibody fragments; flumazenil; intravenous fat emulsion; N-acetylcysteine; naloxone; and octreotide. Each antidote section gives the mechanism, indications, dosing and adverse effects and ends with a paragraph headed Implications for the pharmacist. A recommended antidote stocking list and sample inventory log are in eFigure 1 and eTable 1 at www.ajhp.org.

lecture_use.point: Ethanol or, preferably, fomepizole is given to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) in methanol, ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol poisoning; the parent compounds are relatively nontoxic and ADH metabolizes them to the toxic metabolites. In the transcript she says 'omeprazole' where she means fomepizole.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Antidotes for toxic-alcohol poisoning, p. 200 (first two paragraphs)
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: So, I've got listed on the bottom of the slide here that there's an antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol, and you can use ethanol or now a drug called omeprazole.

lecture_use.point: Methanol is metabolized via ADH to formic acid, which results in anion-gap metabolic acidosis and ocular toxicity; retinal toxicity secondary to methanol poisoning is usually irreversible.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Formic acid will cause damage, especially to the eyes, to the retina of the eyes.

lecture_use.point: Ethylene glycol is metabolized via ADH to glycolic acid (anion-gap metabolic acidosis) and oxalic acid, which results primarily in renal toxicity due to the formation of calcium oxalate crystals.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Well, oxalic acid is a, is a small molecule, and, um, uh, it will sometimes precipitate in the blood to form small microcrystals and The impact of that is you can damage your organs like your liver, your kidneys.

lecture_use.point: Ethanol can be given intravenously or orally, but a commercial i.v. preparation is no longer available; a loading dose is needed to reach a serum ethanol concentration of 100-150 mg/dL, then a maintenance dose guided by repeated serum ethanol measurements.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: So they would use Everclear, have a shot glass there and give somebody that's had methanol or ethylene glycol exposure a shot, maybe two of Everclear, and watch to see how they're doing, OK?

lecture_use.point: Fomepizole's ease of administration and relative lack of serious adverse effects have elevated it to preferred status over ethanol; its advantages are a much higher potency of ADH inhibition (Ki = 0.1 µmol/L, a 1000-fold higher affinity than that of ethanol), better maintenance of therapeutic blood concentrations, fewer adverse effects and less labor-intensive administration.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: We now have, uh, the medication omeprazole that we'll give to patients. Um, a little bit better control of the dosing.

lecture_use.point: Methanol or ethylene glycol toxicity should be suspected in a patient with anion-gap metabolic acidosis in whom laboratory testing reveals a low (or no) ethanol concentration, no ketones, and a normal lactic acid concentration; the availability of testing for toxic alcohols is limited.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Antidotes for toxic-alcohol poisoning, Implications for the pharmacist, p. 201
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: The, the, the, the key indicator would be you get them into the ER and they do a blood draw, and they look for these alcohols in their blood.

lecture_use.point: Urinary alkalinization (a urine pH of >8) with i.v. sodium bicarbonate enhances formate elimination and may reduce the distribution of formic acid to the eye.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: We'll hang a bag of sodium bicarb on a patient, that'll make their urine a bit more basic, which means the pH is elevating, right?

lecture_use.point: Hemodialysis should be considered in all toxic-alcohol exposures in which toxic metabolites have already formed, and empirically if the serum methanol concentration is >25 mg/dL or the serum ethylene glycol concentration is >50 mg/dL with renal insufficiency.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: What this means is you're going to try to artificially clear the blood of toxins, so maybe using hemodialysis, hemofiltration, or hemo perfusion.

lecture_use.point: Cyanide binds to the ferric ion on cytochrome oxidase and abruptly halts the electron transport chain and aerobic respiration.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Cytochrome C oxidase is its target. Anybody know what cytochrome cytochrome C oxidase does? Think back to biochemistry. Helps with our electron transport chain, right?

lecture_use.point: The mechanism of amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite is to produce methemoglobinemia; cyanide bound to cytochrome oxidase is then preferentially bound to methemoglobin, forming cyanomethemoglobin. Amyl nitrite is inhaled pending i.v. access; sodium nitrite is given intravenously and produces a methemoglobin concentration of about 15% in healthy adults.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite, p. 203
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: And methemoglobin is able to pull cyanide off of cytochrome C oxidase. So here's the cyanide. It's going to get pulled off of the cytochrome C oxidase, and it gets stuck onto your methemoglobin, creating cyanoetthemoglobin, OK?

lecture_use.point: Neither carboxyhemoglobin nor methemoglobin is capable of carrying oxygen, so patients can develop functional hypoxia; the nitrite component should be avoided in smoke inhalation unless the carboxyhemoglobin level is shown to be negligible, and a methemoglobin concentration above 20% should halt further nitrite administration.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Is methemoglobin helpful to our bodies? Will it carry oxygen? No, OK, we're still gonna create it in our patients though, because we're trying to save them from their cyanide poisoning, OK?

lecture_use.point: Rhodanese, an endogenous enzyme, facilitates the formation of thiocyanate, a much less toxic metabolite that is renally excreted; this pathway is capacity limited, and sodium thiosulfate (12.5 g i.v. for adults) enhances rhodanese activity by donating a sulfur group. The article names sodium thiosulfate as the administered antidote and rhodanese as the patient's own enzyme.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Antidotes for cyanide poisoning, p. 203; Sodium thiosulfate, p. 204
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: So by giving rodonase as a cofactor, we pull the cyanide off of methemoglobin onto the thiosulfate, and this will be renally eliminated.

lecture_use.point: While acetaminophen is still present in the plasma, NAC acts as an antidote primarily by replenishing glutathione stores; secondarily it acts as a glutathione substitute and replenishes sulfate, limiting formation of the toxic metabolite or detoxifying it.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: But one of the things we can do in this situation is give NA andactylcysteine, cause NA provides some of the ingredients needed to create more glutathione.

lecture_use.point: Both the i.v. and oral routes are believed to be equally efficacious when NAC is given within eight hours of an acetaminophen overdose; oral NAC frequently causes nausea and vomiting and the dose must be repeated if emesis occurs within one hour; i.v. NAC can cause anaphylactoid reactions, particularly with the loading dose.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: So, in the United States, we tend to give it by IV because it's pretty hard to get somebody to swallow something that smells like rotten eggs, and it's kind of oily and, it's a clear liquid, it's kind of disgusting.

lecture_use.point: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram predicts hepatotoxicity from an initial plasma acetaminophen concentration obtained four or more hours after a single acute ingestion; NAC is started when the level is on or above the nomogram, when no level is available within eight hours of a potentially toxic ingestion, or when hepatotoxicity is present.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Can you think of any other compounds that it's likely emergency rooms would test a person's blood for to see if they've been exposed to them? Acetaminophen, OK, acetaminophen.

lecture_use.point: One of the pharmacist's four roles listed in the abstract is managing the procurement and stocking of antidotes to ensure their timely availability; some antidotes must be stocked in the ED for immediate administration and others must be available within 60 minutes.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Has anybody, um, just for fun, anybody ever, uh, been in a hospital where they have, maybe you work in a hospital pharmacy and you've had to stock, uh, NAStylcysteine?

lecture_use.point: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) are lifesaving agents in toxicity from digoxin and other cardioactive steroids, including digitoxin and those derived from oleander, fox glove, lily of the valley, and toad venom. The article does not use the word monoclonal.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: And then the antibody that we have is the example I have here is digoxin immune fab. This is an antibody, a monoclonal antibody that's made to treat a digoxin overdose, OK?

lecture_use.point: Each 38- or 40-mg vial of digoxin-specific Fab binds 0.5 mg of digoxin; empiric dosing is 10-20 vials for acute toxicity and 3-5 vials (adults) or 1-2 vials (children) for chronic toxicity. After Fab is given, serum digoxin concentrations are no longer useful because the total digoxin concentration rises, so repeat levels should not be obtained for 24 hours.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: One form of antibody made to grab digoxin that somebody's overdosed on, it grabs it and nicely clears it out of the blood.

lecture_use.point: Naloxone, the most commonly used antidote in the ED setting, is a competitive antagonist at all opioid receptors, including the µ-opioid receptor; an initial dose of 0.04-0.05 mg i.v. titrated upward is recommended, and its clinical effect lasts 30-90 minutes.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Naloxone is basically an antagonist of an opioid receptor

lecture_use.point: Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine-receptor binding site on γ-aminobutyric acid-A. The article discourages its use in overdose patients unless it is certain that only a benzodiazepine was ingested and the patient is not benzodiazepine dependent and has no seizure history, because it can precipitate withdrawal seizures and unmask arrhythmias in mixed ingestions.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Flonazanil is used commonly for, uh, overdoses of things like your benzodiazepines. The, uh, benzos are gonna be agonizing your GABA receptors, right, causing a lot of, a lot of action on that, that receptor, and flomazanil will antagonize the GABA receptor, OK?

lecture_use.point: Benzodiazepine overdose produces a toxidrome, or toxic syndrome, of CNS depression with relatively normal vital signs; deaths attributed solely to oral benzodiazepine ingestion are rare.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: Usually you'll see a group of systems of symptoms that we call a toxic toxodrome that we'll get to at the end of this lecture, kind of a group of symptoms that are like, oh hey, look, this person has this, this and this.

lecture_use.point: Because of the pathophysiologic similarities of CCB toxicity and β-blocker toxicity, their management is similar (fluids and atropine first, then calcium, glucagon, HIET, vasopressors, cardiac pacing, i.v. 20% fatty acid emulsion, extracorporeal circulatory support, intra-aortic balloon pump). Presenting symptoms differ: CCB overdose patients tend to remain awake and alert, β-blocker patients are more likely to have altered mental status and respiratory depression, and severe CCB overdose causes hyperglycemia.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Antidotes for calcium-channel-blocker and β-blocker toxicities, p. 201
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: These are both cardiac meds, slightly different time frames that speaks to the mechanism of action of calcium channel blockers versus beta blockers

lecture_use.point: Clinicians should always consult a regional poison control center (1-800-222-1222) to ascertain the most current recommendations on antidote use and to report exposures and poisonings.
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: this is where the poison center will guide you on whether you need to get them to the emergency room, or you need to call the ambulance, OK?

lecture_use.point: The article's evidence for several antidotes is case reports and animal studies: for intravenous fat emulsion, research remains in the discovery phase despite promising case reports, and for octreotide there are no published data from randomized clinical trials.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Intravenous fat emulsion, p. 206; Octreotide, p. 208
lecture_use.lecture_evidence: we really can't run clinical trials and sign up people to volunteer to get poisoned and try to see what treatment works best for them

read_for: Antidotes for toxic-alcohol poisoning (p. 200): methanol to formic acid (anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ocular toxicity, usually irreversible retinal toxicity); ethylene glycol to glycolic acid and oxalic acid (renal toxicity from calcium oxalate crystals); diethylene glycol to hydroxyethoxyacetic acid and diglycolic acid; about 5000 exposures and 20-30 deaths a year.

Ethanol (p. 200): competitive ADH inhibition, target serum ethanol 100-150 mg/dL, loading dose then maintenance dose with repeated serum ethanol checks, no commercial i.v. preparation; risks of CNS depression, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting, phlebitis.

Fomepizole (p. 200): FDA regimen of 15 mg/kg i.v. over 30 minutes, then 10 mg/kg every 12 hours, every 4 hours during hemodialysis, and 15 mg/kg every 12 hours after 48 hours; Ki 0.1 µmol/L (1000-fold higher affinity than ethanol); half-lives of ethylene glycol and methanol of 14.5 and 40 hours in its presence.

Additional and supportive therapy (p. 200) and Implications for the pharmacist (p. 201): hemodialysis criteria (methanol >25 mg/dL; ethylene glycol >50 mg/dL with renal insufficiency); folic acid 50 mg i.v. every six hours; urinary alkalinization to pH >8 with sodium bicarbonate; thiamine 100 mg and pyridoxine 50 mg; the lab pattern that should raise suspicion (anion-gap acidosis, low or no ethanol, no ketones, normal lactate).

Antidotes for cyanide poisoning (p. 203): cyanide binds the ferric ion on cytochrome oxidase and halts the electron transport chain; sources (house fires, industrial accidents, suicide attempts, chemical warfare); lactate >8 mmol/L and high venous oxygen saturation as suggestive findings; nitrites produce methemoglobinemia and cyanomethemoglobin; sodium nitrite 300 mg (10 mL of 3%) i.v. for adults, 6 mg/kg for children; stop nitrites above 20% methemoglobin.

Sodium thiosulfate (p. 204): rhodanese forms thiocyanate, thiosulfate donates a sulfur group, adult dose 12.5 g i.v. (50 mL of 25% solution), pediatric 0.5 g/kg, given after sodium nitrite via the same line; recommended for all patients with suspected cyanide toxicity including smoke inhalation.

N-acetylcysteine (p. 206-207): replenishes glutathione stores, acts as a glutathione substitute and replenishes sulfate; Rumack-Matthew nomogram with a level drawn four or more hours after ingestion; i.v. 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, 100 mg/kg over 16 hours (21-hour regimen, continue 6.25 mg/kg/hr if needed); oral 140 mg/kg then 70 mg/kg every four hours for 17 doses; nearly 100% hepatoprotective within the first eight hours; i.v. NAC decreased mortality by 50% in acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure.

Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (p. 204-205): indications (symptomatic bradycardia or heart block unresponsive to atropine, ventricular arrhythmias, serum potassium >5.0 meq/L, ingestion of >4 mg by a child or >10 mg by an adult, chronic level >2.5 ng/mL with symptoms); each 38- or 40-mg vial binds 0.5 mg digoxin; empiric 10-20 vials acute, 3-5 vials chronic; vial calculation = concentration (ng/mL) x weight (kg) / 100; serum digoxin levels unusable for 24 hours afterward; avoid calcium in digoxin toxicity (p. 202).

Flumazenil (p. 205-206) and Naloxone (p. 208): flumazenil as competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A, its withdrawal-seizure and mixed-ingestion risks, 0.2 mg/min dosing and 3 mg/hour ceiling; naloxone as competitive antagonist at all opioid receptors, 0.04-0.05 mg starting dose titrated to 10 mg, 30-90 minute duration, infusion at two-thirds of the effective hourly dose, higher doses for synthetic opioids and bell-shaped response with buprenorphine.

Antidotes for calcium-channel-blocker and β-blocker toxicities, introduction (p. 201): hypotension, bradycardia, conduction block and myocardial depression; CCB patients awake and alert versus β-blocker altered mental status and respiratory depression; hyperglycemia with severe CCB overdose; propranolol's lipophilicity and sodium-channel blockade causing seizures and widened QRS; combined CCB and β-blocker ingestion is particularly serious.
beyond_lecture: Calcium (p. 202): 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate equals 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride; calcium chloride through a central line because of extravasation injury; starting dose and repeat doses at 15-20 minutes; ionized calcium monitoring after three doses - not covered in lecture.

Glucagon (p. 202): raises cardiac cAMP independently of the β-adrenergic receptor; 50 µg/kg, or 3-5 mg up to a cumulative 10 mg, then infusion; nausea, vomiting, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia; duration rarely longer than 15 minutes - not covered in lecture.

HIET, hyperinsulinemia-euglycemia therapy (p. 202): 1 unit/kg regular insulin load then 0.5-1 unit/kg/hr, increased every 20-30 minutes, doses of 2.5-3 units/kg/hr used; dextrose 0.5 g/kg load and 0.5 g/kg/hr with a glucose goal of 100-250 mg/dL; start when calcium and glucagon fail or a vasopressor is being started - not covered in lecture.

Hydroxocobalamin (p. 204): vitamin B12a that forms cyanocobalamin, renally excreted; 5 g i.v. over 15 minutes for adults, 70 mg/kg for children; preferred for smoke inhalation because it does not compromise oxygen-carrying capacity or cause hypotension; chromaturia and interference with colorimetric laboratory tests and carboxyhemoglobin determinations - the lecture's cyanide scheme used amyl nitrite, rhodanese/thiosulfate and methylene blue and did not mention hydroxocobalamin.

Intravenous fat emulsion (p. 206): lipid sink theory; first-line for bupivacaine cardiotoxicity and considered for lipophilic cardiotoxic drugs (tricyclic antidepressants, verapamil, diltiazem, bupropion, propranolol); 20% IFE 100 mL (1.5 mL/kg) i.v. push, optional infusion 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min; not FDA approved for this use - not covered in lecture.

Octreotide (p. 208-209): somatostatin analog that inhibits pancreatic insulin release for sulfonylurea- and miglitinide-induced hypoglycemia; 50 µg subcutaneously every six hours as needed after dextrose 0.5-1 g/kg - not covered in lecture.

Introduction and supplementary material (p. 199-200): the national consensus list of 24 antidotes, ED versus 60-minute availability, eFigure 1 stocking list and eTable 1 inventory log - not covered in lecture.

The poisoning treatment table built from this article (signs and symptoms of overdose, antidote, antidote mechanism) is due the morning of 10/20; she said 'we'll go over the table tomorrow morning in the beginning of class' and 'Once everybody has turned in their table to me tomorrow morning, I will post my key'.

terms.chapter_definition: Fomepizole competitively inhibits ADH and is an effective and safe antidote for both ethylene glycol and methanol toxicity; in its presence the half-lives of ethylene glycol (in patients with normal renal function) and methanol are 14.5 and 40 hours, respectively.

For many years, ethanol has been used to inhibit ADH and limit the metabolism of methanol and ethylene glycol to their respective metabolites; most authorities recommend a dose sufficient to achieve and maintain a serum ethanol concentration of 100-150 mg/dL.

High-dose insulin therapy for patients severely poisoned with CCBs or β-blockers; the available data suggest it enhances carbohydrate use and energy production by myocardial cells, resulting in improved contractility, with benefits delayed 15-60 minutes.
An endogenous enzyme that facilitates the formation of thiocyanate, a much less toxic metabolite of cyanide, which is renally excreted; this metabolic pathway is capacity limited.
Thiosulfate enhances the activity of rhodanese by donating a sulfur group, thereby increasing the amount of thiocyanate that rhodanese can produce; adult dose 12.5 g i.v. (50 mL of 25% solution).
Vitamin B12a; it detoxifies cyanide and forms cyanocobalamin, which is renally excreted; it does not compromise the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and does not produce hypotension.

Lifesaving agents in the management of toxicity associated with the use of digoxin and other cardioactive steroids, including digitoxin and those derived from oleander, fox glove, lily of the valley, and toad venom; each 38- or 40-mg vial binds 0.5 mg of digoxin.

A competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine-receptor binding site on γ-aminobutyric acid-A; its use in overdose patients is discouraged unless only a benzodiazepine was ingested and the patient is not benzodiazepine dependent and has no history of seizure.
A toxidrome, or toxic syndrome; for benzodiazepines ingested in overdose, CNS depression with relatively normal vital signs.
While acetaminophen is still present in the plasma, NAC acts as an antidote, primarily by replenishing glutathione stores; secondarily, it acts as a glutathione substitute and replenishes sulfate.

Used to predict whether patients will develop hepatotoxicity, defined as a serum AST concentration of >1000 units/L, based on an initial plasma acetaminophen concentration obtained four or more hours after a single acute ingestion of acetaminophen.

The most commonly used antidote in the ED setting; a competitive antagonist at all opioid receptors, including the µ-opioid receptor, and a well-established antidote for respiratory depression secondary to opioid toxicity.

listen: This reading is "Antidotes for toxicological emergencies: A practical review," by Jeanna Marraffa, Victor Cohen and Mary Ann Howland, in the American Journal of Health System Pharmacy, 2012. It reviews the antidotes for common poisonings, with each one's mechanism, indications, dosing and adverse effects. These rows of her poisoning table key come from it, in her key's wording. Acetaminophen: nausea and vomiting, clinical signs of liver failure, and blood levels can be measured. N acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione. It loses effectiveness about eight hours after the overdose, and you should still give it past that point. Toxic alcohols: methanol's active metabolites cause anion gap metabolic acidosis and ocular toxicity. Ethylene glycol's metabolites can crystallize in the microvasculature, and renal toxicity is common. Ethanol or fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase. Fomepizole is the stronger inhibitor and has fewer adverse effects. Benzodiazepines: central nervous system depression with relatively normal vital signs. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist of the benzodiazepine receptor, and it can cause withdrawal in a benzodiazepine dependent patient. Beta blockers: hypotension, bradycardia, altered mental status, and respiratory depression. Atropine increases heart rate. Calcium tries to drive calcium into cardiac cells. Glucagon increases cardiac cyclic A M P to increase heart rate. For hyperinsulinemia euglycemia therapy, the mechanism of the inotropic effect is not understood. Vasopressors raise blood pressure. Intravenous twenty percent fat emulsion acts as a sink for a lipophilic drug. Calcium channel blockers: hypotension and bradycardia, but often alert, with the same antidotes. Digoxin: bradycardia, arrhythmias, elevated serum potassium, nausea and vomiting. Digoxin specific antibody fragments bind digoxin, which is then renally eliminated. After the antidote, the total digoxin level, free plus bound, goes up, so it can't be used to calculate more doses. Opioids: somnolence, coma, slower heart and breathing rates, and small pupils. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist of opioid receptors and can trigger withdrawal in chronic users. Sulfonylureas and meglitinides: hypoglycemia, treated with octreotide, which inhibits insulin release from the pancreas. Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase and halts the electron transport chain. Nitrites create methemoglobin, which pulls cyanide off cytochrome oxidase. Rhodanese, helped by sulfur from sodium thiosulfate, forms thiocyanate, which the kidneys excrete. The traps. N acetylcysteine supplies ingredients for glutathione. She told a student, "No, it's not neutralizing free radicals." Glucagon raises cyclic A M P. It is not a cofactor. Rhodanese is the body's own enzyme, and sodium thiosulfate is the drug given. In class she called digoxin immune Fab "a monoclonal antibody." The product is ovine, made in sheep. Opioid overdose shrinks the pupils, so larger pupils are not part of it.
